The Brown snake eagle (Circaetus cinereus) is a large raptor found across sub-Saharan Africa, where it occupies savanna and open woodland habitats. Field studies of this species have documented key reproductive parameters under typical thermal conditions of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. Observational records indicate that females produce a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch] and raise just one clutch annually [F_R_i = one clutch annually], a minimal reproductive output that reflects the high energetic costs of incubating and provisioning a single, rapidly growing chick. Interestingly, adult males of this species attain an ultimate wet body mass of 2028 grams [Wwi = 2028 grams], a value consistently observed across multiple study populations in southern and eastern Africa. These reproductive parameters, combined with the slow maturation typical of large raptors, position the species as an extreme K-strategist among Afrotropical woodland birds.

Hatchling brown snake eagles emerge from eggs that have been incubated for approximately 52.8 days [ab = approximately 52.8 days] at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a protracted incubation period typical of accipitrid raptors of similar body size. At the moment of hatching, neonates weigh approximately 100 grams [Wwb = approximately 100 grams], a relatively modest initial mass that nonetheless represents a substantial energetic investment from the parents given the single-egg clutch. The initial wet weight of the developing embryo within the freshly laid egg is approximately 139 grams [Ww0 = approximately 139 grams], reflecting the substantial yolk reserves required to support the lengthy developmental period within the shell.

Under field conditions characterised by a mean ambient temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C], the developmental milestones of this species follow a well-defined schedule. The fledging stage, marked by the young bird achieving its first sustained flight from the nest, occurs at 104.5 days after hatching [tx = 104.5 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This relatively extended nestling period allows the chick to attain sufficient flight feather development and motor coordination before independence. Sexual maturity, defined by the onset of gonadal activity and the ability to breed, is reached at 313.5 days after hatching [tp = 313.5 days after hatching], although most individuals do not immediately secure a territory or find a mate at this age at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C].

Age at first successful reproduction, meaning the production of a viable clutch that leads to fledged young, is typically deferred until approximately 3 years after hatching [tR = approximately 3 years after hatching] under a mean ambient temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This delay of about three years from hatching to first breeding is characteristic of large-bodied raptors with low adult mortality rates. The extended pre-reproductive period likely reflects the time required to acquire the hunting skills, territory ownership, and pair-bond stability necessary for successful reproduction. This slow pace of life history, combined with the single-egg clutch, makes the population particularly sensitive to declines in adult survival.

The maximum lifespan recorded for the brown snake eagle in wild populations, again under a mean ambient temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C], is approximately 6.8 years [am = approximately 6.8 years]. This longevity, while modest compared to some other large raptors, is consistent with its relatively slow life-history strategy. Adult females attain a greater ultimate body mass than males, reaching an asymptotic mass of 2048 grams [Wwi = 2048 grams], a difference presumably linked to the energetic demands of egg production and extended incubation. The combination of a single-egg clutch, a protracted developmental period, and a moderately long lifespan places Circaetus cinereus among the slower-reproducing accipitrids, a strategy that appears well-suited to the unpredictable prey availability of its savanna habitat.
